en: The Heart Sutra explains that in the cultivation of the myriad practices for the liberation of the mind, wisdom is paramount. Yet, if one fails to clarify *prajñā*, it is like reaching the edge of a precipice while still clinging to a raft;

thus, the First Patriarch came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature one may become a Buddha, thereby continuing the life of wisdom. This lineage was transmitted five times until it reached Huangmei. Then—

This refers specifically to human beings. To receive and uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is, by virtue of what is expressed through *prajñā*, precisely what the First Patriarch directly pointed out.

There is no duality between the Teaching (*jiao*) and the School (*zong*). However, when that which is spoken of in the Teaching is put into practice, it becomes the grandmotherly compassion of the Patriarch’s mind;
when that which is practiced in the School is articulated in speech, it becomes the broad and long tongue of the Buddha. Therefore:

There is merely a distinction in the names of religions. Alas, since ancient times, people have distinguished between "Tathāgata Chan" and "Patriarchal Chan," using practice as a criterion for inclusion or exclusion.
Those who follow the stream of deluded words have consequently venerated Patriarchal Chan as the ultimate standard, while setting aside Tathāgata Chan without further inquiry.
Moreover, that which they venerate as Patriarchal Chan is not the Patriarchal Chan of antiquity; it is simply nothing more than...
His witty sayings are novel and his phrasing possesses a distinct cadence. Compared to a learned abbot who merely recites the words of others, he is like a painter:
one paints birds and beasts, while the other paints ghosts and monsters; though both are painters, they never depart from their brush and ink, yet each possesses a unique spiritual skill.
What is there to marvel at? Furthermore, as for birds and beasts, people have long seen them in reality; whether a painting of them is similar or dissimilar is difficult to deceive others with.
However, ghosts and spirits are rarely seen by people; whether a painting of them is similar or dissimilar cannot be distinguished as erroneous.

Therefore, the decline of our school's style is even more severe than that of the lecture halls. I hope that those who boast of being Chan practitioners will be clearly realized in the Tathāgata-dhyāna, and not merely [in name].
It can be understood thus: even if Huishan were raised up today, he would say, "As for the Zen of the Patriarchs, I grant you its mastery;
as for the Zen of the Tathāgata, you have not yet dreamed of it. This is not because he holds the Zen of the Tathāgata high and the Zen of the Patriarchs low.
The Dharma-gate is thus. To whom can the life of wisdom be entrusted? Since the life of wisdom has no place of entrustment, who today can deliver it?

Dwelling in the mountains with nothing to do, I occasionally take up the Mahāyāna sūtras and teachings to show them to my disciples. This is because, as long as one has not yet reached the point of speaking, how could one possibly reach the point of practice?
If one wishes to speak to the point, it cannot be done except through the words of the broad and long tongue.
Relying on the indications of the sutras, I shall briefly borrow these words of the broad and long tongue to advance all people toward the Tathāgata-dhyāna, so as to reach the Patriarchal-dhyāna.

This is not because I am willing to leave people merely at the level of the Tathāgata-dhyāna, nor is it that I would fail to lead them to the Patriarchal-dhyāna. If there should be anyone who takes this up...

Carrying it away, the hot rod is merciless; I have not yet released you. Now, because of a disciple who has newly resolved his mind, named Kaidu (Opening and Delivering), he was reciting and upholding [this text] at that time, and I provided him with its commentary and explanation. For this reason, I have given him the name Kaidu.

To "privately appropriate the Prajñā" is to take the foremost of the six perfections and the myriad practices, as transmitted by the four and seven patriarchs of the Western Heaven (India) and the two and three patriarchs of the Eastern Land (China).
Chishi Shi resides here. If one truly wishes to enlighten and deliver those who come to study, what else could be used but this?

Since the original intention was to enlighten and deliver through discourse, it is fitting that the title be designated as "Kaidu" (Enlightenment and Deliverance). Written by the monk Luofeng Duodao of Xin'an, for the *Heart Sutra Kaidu*.
Written by the Śramaṇa of Xin’an, Shi Luofeng Hongli. *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. *Prajñā* is a Sanskrit term;

here it is translated as "wisdom. These two characters represent the function and the cause. *Pāramitā*... [is]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "波羅蜜多" (*pāramitā*). The full title would typically continue with "彼岸到" (*to the other shore*) or "度" (*crossing over*), signifying the perfection of wisdom.)
In the Sanskrit language, this is called *pāramitā*, which here means "reaching the other shore. These three characters represent the verification, the fruit, and the efficacy:

where there is efficacy, there is verification; where there is a cause, there is a fruit; and where there is wisdom, one reaches the other shore. This is because birth and death constitute this shore.
It is all due to the deluded vision of ignorance (*avidyā*). If there were no ignorance, there would be no "this shore" of birth and death;

this itself is the arrival at the "other shore. It is not that there is some separate other shore to be reached. Because there is primordial ignorance, one loses fundamental luminous wisdom (*prajñā*), becomes confused regarding non-existence, clings to existence, and gives rise to deluded cognition and views, thereby establishing this shore of birth and death. Therefore...
Thus one achieves the crossing to the other shore. If one does not lose wisdom, how could there be ignorance?
How could there be this shore of birth and death? Would it not be the case that every person reaches the other shore of nirvana?
Therefore, wisdom must be taken as the cause; from this arises the fruit of reaching the other shore. This is the Prajñāpāramitā. (Repetition of text)
The meaning of the phrases is as follows. If one asks what constitutes wisdom (*prajñā*), the subsequent scriptural passage provides a clear exposition.

One should analyze this for oneself when encountering the text; however, to state the essential point: to illuminate the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*) and to be without attainment—that is wisdom.
If one does not illuminate the emptiness of the aggregates and perceives nothing to be attained, that is not wisdom; it is ignorance. Ignorance is the absence of the light of wisdom.
Therefore, one is unable to accept non-attainment with equanimity and, being deluded, sees existence where there is none. To be able to remain without the notion of existence is clarity.
It is like the sky when there are no clouds—it is bright and clear; or like a door or window being opened—it is filled with light.
Liang: When a person is free from attachment, they attain penetration; this is all evidenced by the realization of non-attainment.
Yet people today are attached to existence in every thought-moment—how could they possibly achieve clarity? Thus, they are nothing but ignorant sentient beings;
they are nothing but those transmigrating through birth and death, unable to reach the other shore. Those who hear this sutra should be struck with awe and awakened. [The] mind.

The single character "this" (zhi) is a metaphor. It serves as a metaphor for how this sutra encompasses the beginning and end within the four hundred fascicles of the Prajñāpāramitā section, acting as the fundamental source of the entire Prajñāpāramitā corpus.
It is like the heart within the human body, which is the sovereign of the hundred limbs and myriad apertures.
If a person can control the heart, they can govern the physical form; likewise, if one can thoroughly penetrate this sutra, then—
The entire Prajñā is thoroughly penetrated; there is no other meaning. Therefore, the character *xin* (心) is used as a metaphor for illumination.

The character *jing* (經) carries the sense of threading together and encompassing, like a thread passing through flowers to gather them into a garland for adornment, thereby manifesting the Buddha’s teachings.
The Dharma-gate for Gathering the Multitude; the Cultivation and Realization of Buddhahood; furthermore, the Instruction on the Constant and the Instruction on the Dharma:
these refer to the Buddha’s teachings as the eternal, constant Dharma that must never be contravened. This constitutes the further praise of all the Buddhas’ bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.
By understanding them through this [method], one will, upon encountering the titles of the sutras, [comprehend] the subsequent textual passages.
One may then consider that more than half [of the task] has already been accomplished. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
through this person, manifests the teaching and establishes a model for sentient beings, causing them to act as the Bodhisattva does.
This is the profoundly deep Prajñā. Now, Prajñā is the cause of the Buddha-fruit and the common path traversed by all Bodhisattvas;

why then is this teaching specifically based upon the Bodhisattva? It is because the Bodhisattva fundamentally realized the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, thereby attesting to the non-arising of nature and bringing forth the manifestation of quiescent extinction. This is that through which ignorance is destroyed, and this is wisdom.
This is that from which [wisdom] arises. To see this Bodhisattva is to see wisdom itself. Therefore, what is its unique foundation? Why is this so?

All phenomena are merely verbal designations; they possess no substantial reality at all. To be deluded by them and fail to understand is to follow after sounds and flow in transmigration—this is ignorance (*avidyā*).
To awaken to them and be able to understand is for hearing to clear away the obscuration—this is wisdom (*prajñā*). Now...
The Bodhisattva’s original name is Avalokiteśvara. He contemplates the world as being like an echo; how could there be any objective grasping?
Seeking out sounds to rescue beings from their manifold sufferings, how could he be deluded regarding reality? Thus, ignorance is immediately shattered and wisdom is born. Therefore it is said:
"The true essence of the teaching in this land lies in the purity of hearing sounds. If one does not take this Bodhisattva as the foundation, what else could serve as the foundation?
Ah! Alas! Do you people wish to attain Avalokiteśvara? Seek Avalokitasvara.
Or rather, by contemplating the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha-śūnyatā*), when the mind becomes free from obstruction, that itself is Avalokiteśvara; this, too, is Avalokiteśvara.
This is precisely Prajñā. Since there are no two distinct dharmas, it alone is taken as the root to manifest the teaching.
When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, this is the fundamental essence of the Bodhisattva;
it is the name of the Dharma that emerges during the cultivation of the mind on the causal ground. As for what is called "profound *prajñā*," it is...
The contemplation that form is itself emptiness is the manifest quiescence of ultimate nirvana;

it is the direct realization of the Buddha-fruit’s perfect and universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), not the provisional and inferior vehicle of the *śrāvakas*. It is not something that can be reached through shallow or superficial observation and understanding. The practitioner relies upon *prajñā*.

Entering the stream, one forgets the object; one does not fall into the conditioned, nor does one abide in the unconditioned. "Time" refers to the periods of the initial, middle, and final minds during the cultivation and realization on the causal ground.

"To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty" is truly the contemplative insight arising from the profound *prajñā*. These characters "perceive" (*zhào jiàn*) are identical to the character "practice" (*xíng*) [in the title *The Perfection of Wisdom*].

However, it does not mean perceiving one thing as empty in isolation; rather, by practicing *prajñā*, one simply realizes that the five aggregates lack any substantial nature, and do not [arise] through... [causes].
From this, deluded conceptualization arises, establishing the duality of subject and object, and creating the causes and effects of saṃsāra.

This is the mirror of wisdom that illuminates emptiness; this is the practice of Prajñā. Regarding the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—they are fundamentally the two aspects of the eight consciousnesses:

the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiving (darśana-bhāga). Based on these, the two dharmas of matter and mind are established; within the mind, the four factors of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are distinguished.

The name "five aggregates" (skandhas) is established because they shroud sentient beings with the five hindrances, causing them to lose their original nature—the wondrous, luminous awakening—and thus they are called "aggregates.

As for "form" (rūpa): it refers to all external and internal physical forms, including the sense organs, the body, and the environmental world. As for "feeling" (vedanā): internally, it is the defiled attachment to the sense organs and the body;
externally, it is the increase of craving for the environmental world. As for "perception" (saṃjñā): internally, it is the mental deliberation and conceptualization; externally...

Regarding the distinction based on objects: as for the practitioner, internally there is the arising and ceasing of mental factors (*caitta*), and externally there is the transformation of appearances;

as for consciousness (*vijñāna*), internally there is the sovereign awareness and cognition, and externally there are images, forms, and colors. This is spoken from the perspective of how objects arise from the mind.

Then there is consciousness; from this there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). When there are volitional formations, perception (*saṃjñā*) is formed. With perception as its basis, sensation (*vedanā*) arises.
Speaking in terms of the mind arising from objects, sensation gives rise to perception, perception constitutes volitional formations, and volitional formations manifest consciousness.
These four are mutually the beginning and the end; this is what is called the fundamental ignorance that moistens rebirth. If these four were not present, then...

There is no [self] in form. If there is no [self] in form, how could there be the four [aggregates]? Furthermore, these two divisions—the characteristic and the observer—are the beginning and the end [of cyclic existence].
Now, it is said that all are empty; thus, one perceives that a single dharma is illusory, and consequently, every dharma is illusory.
All phenomena are illusory; in reality, there is not a single phenomenon that arises. Encompassing the faculties, objects, realms, and emptiness, there are no phenomena of birth and death within.
Since there are no phenomena of the birth and death of sentient beings, how could there be the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?
Since there are no phenomena of the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, how could there be the Single Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas?

The Dharma is fully encompassed within this. Therefore, this contemplative insight constitutes the profound Prajñāpāramitā. As for how one should contemplate and observe, it will be explained in the subsequent text.
It delivers one from all suffering and calamity.
This is truly the basis from which [wisdom] emerges; it is the arrival at the other shore by means of *prajñā*. Suffering and calamity constitute this shore;

crossing over suffering and calamity is the departure from this shore and the arrival at the other shore. "All" refers to all forms of birth-and-death, both *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative).
Indeed, ordinary beings who revolve in saṃsāra experience the suffering and calamity of segmented birth-and-death, as they are deluded regarding the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha-śūnyatā*).

[The practitioner] stands [in this realization]. Those who have attained a shallow realization of the Sage fear the suffering and calamities of *pariṇāma-śūnyatā* (the death-rebirth cycle of subtle transformation), yet they do not establish themselves in the ultimate emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha-śūnyatā*). Now, by deeply illuminating the emptiness of the aggregates, one attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*;
thus, one crosses over all suffering and calamity. Therefore, those people of today who do not escape from suffering and calamity are all binding themselves. If one can...
Contemplating the emptiness of the aggregates, one does not harbor the fear of birth and death characteristic of the two vehicles, but rather delivers sentient beings according to their kinds;
how much less would one dwell in attachment to birth and death like an ordinary person? This is the revelation of the true principle for crossing over suffering and calamity.
However, it must be understood that the "suffering and calamity" to be crossed over in this sutra refers to the Bodhisattva’s deliverance of all sentient beings from [samsara].
This refers to suffering and distress. If one were to explain this solely as a discourse on transcending one's own suffering and distress, one would miss the point.

Taken together, these constitute the main text that reveals the Dharma through the person. All subsequent passages are the words of the Buddha for Śāriputra, intended to clarify and reveal the profound Prajñā that transcends suffering and distress by bringing about the realization that the aggregates are empty.
Śāriputra: This is the name of a disciple who was suited to the occasion. Śāri is a Sanskrit word; here it means "śārikā," which is a bird.
This bird has the most brilliant and keen eyesight. The Venerable One’s mother had eyes like those of this bird, and thus he was named after her. The Venerable One relied upon his mother.
He was given the name Śāriputra. Among the Buddha’s śrāvaka disciples, he was foremost in wisdom and capable of realizing the profound Prajñāpāramitā;
therefore, [the Buddha] specifically called upon him and addressed him.
"Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form.
This is taught to reveal the true principle of the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*), which is primordially quiescent and manifest.

It is intended to prevent confusion regarding the Bodhisattva’s contemplative vision that illuminates the emptiness of the aggregates. One phrase points to emptiness as being empty of form; one phrase points to form as being empty.
"Emptiness" refers to emptiness being empty of form, so as to prevent delusion regarding form. "Form" refers to form being empty of emptiness, so as to prevent delusion regarding emptiness.

For if one is deluded about form, one loses emptiness; if one is deluded about emptiness, one is obstructed by form. To lose the realm that is free from obstruction is to possess a mind subject to change and transition.
To grasp at illumination without constancy is precisely a cognition characterized by arising and ceasing; it is not the perfect, luminous illumination of profound Prajñā.
It is seen as such. Therefore, the two are now shown to be non-different, so that one may know that there is no emptiness outside of form, nor form outside of emptiness;
thus, seeing all as form and all as emptiness, and all as emptiness and all as form, the non-dual function is illuminated, and the single path of Nirvana manifests before one.
The principle of their non-difference is indicated in the following two lines, which shall be explained in context.

To be deluded by form belongs to the knowledge and vision of ordinary beings within the cycle of birth and death; to be deluded by emptiness belongs to the knowledge and vision of non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles.
Upon entering the Hall of Prajñā, none of these things exist at all.
"Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form.
This is the teaching that reveals their non-differentiation. Why are they not different? Because they are simply this.

Now, as for "form," it refers to the root-body and the vessel-world (the environment) which are the congealed manifestations of solidified false discrimination. The four great elements are clearly present, as are the mountains...
The river can be seen; why then is it identical to emptiness? Perfect Enlightenment explains this: "This body of mine is a combination of the four great elements.
That which is called hair of the head and body, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, bones, tendons, marrow, brain, and impurities—all these belong to the element of earth.
Saliva, nasal mucus, pus, blood, lymph, spittle, foam, phlegm, tears, semen, vital energy, and the excretions of both large and small bowel—all these..."
Heat returns to fire; movement returns to wind. As the four great elements each depart, where then shall this delusory body reside?
One thus knows that this body ultimately has no substance; it exists as a phenomenon through the conjunction [of elements], truly identical to a magical illusion.
By understanding the meaning of this sutra, one directly penetrates the principle of emptiness within the very form and color of the present four-element body.
Generally speaking, those who perceive the body as having form do so because they assume there is a body formed through combination.

Therefore, the Sūtra directly demonstrates that there is no body formed by combination, in order to eliminate deluded attachments. Now, when various substances combine to form a single entity, the original substances cannot retain their individual forms.
If the original substances were able to retain their forms, then it would mean they had never combined in the first place—just as if one were to take blue and yellow...

If one takes the five colors—red, black, white, and so on—and blends them together to form a composite color, can they not still be distinguished such that the blue returns to blue and the yellow returns to yellow?
Now, you maintain that the body is a combination of the four great elements;

yet within this body, the solid characteristic of the earth element can be pointed out individually and assigned to the earth element, and the moist characteristic of the water element can be pointed out individually and assigned to the water element.
The fire element has the characteristic of heat; each instance can be identified as belonging to the fire element. The wind element has the characteristic of motion;
each instance can be identified as belonging to the wind element. Since each can be so identified, how could they not be distinct? Since they are distinct, wherein could they possibly be combined?
One should know that this body is ultimately without substance. One should know that this body is truly identical to an illusion.

An illusory body is like a body in a dream; the persons within a dream exist yet do not exist. If they existed as something truly existent, why would the persons dreamed of not appear when one has awakened?
If you say that they are born in the dream and perish upon waking, [then their existence is likewise unreal].

Cessation occurs through non-existence. Yet, since the arising of a dream possesses the characteristic of arising and manifests various persons and things, the cessation upon waking should likewise possess the characteristic of cessation, as seen in the withered remains. When people awaken from their dreams, where are those withered persons and things?
Since there is no characteristic of cessation, there is likewise no characteristic of arising. A body without the characteristic of arising possesses form that has the characteristic of arising.
Is it not the case that form is itself emptiness? That people today find it difficult to speak of this is because they are like dreamers who have not heard the sound of thunder.
I am alone in my wonder that when Guifeng read this passage of the *Nirvana Sūtra* on the *Awakening of Faith* many years ago, he wept with such grief and, in that very moment, knew his true home.
Hong Juefan remarked that he had realized what the Stonehead (Shitou) had said regarding the four great elements.
The nature returns to itself. Yet, how is it that in your commentary on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, you have missed the perfect principle of the Sūtra in so many ways?
Even in your explanation of the passage "the four great elements are each separate," you are unable to point directly to the present reality.

By treating "each being separate" as an object of contemplative analysis, is it not because you are still deluded regarding the actual principle of emptiness, like one confused about hemp? Reflect deeply on the reason for this; it must surely stem from...
At that time, within the sūtras, one was merely able to penetrate the delusion but had not yet attained realization of the truth.

If one merely penetrates the delusion without realizing the truth, then it has not been said that the nature of the four great elements returns of itself, nor has it been said that form is itself emptiness.
Why do you not reflect further? Venerable Pūrṇa, on that day you were doubtful that the four great elements could mutually overcome one another and thus fail to be perfectly pervasive.
Yet, in this body of mine today, the four great elements are pervasive;
there is no place that is not solid, no place that is not moist, no place that is not warm, and no place that is not mobile. They have never mutually overcome one another. Why is this? It must be...
As for their great nature, it is like the light of a lamp: though it fills a room, it is not obstructed by the room; therefore, a single room can contain many lamps.
Thus, a single body may accommodate the four elements simultaneously. This can be further verified by observing a sick person:
when one element contracts a disease and loses its own nature, the remaining elements all become unstable. They constantly encounter wind and develop fever, and [the humors] flow...

The flow of tears and pain in the body arise because the great elements (mahābhūtas) are in excess; yet each of these great elements possesses its own nature, which they then mutually encroach upon and usurp.
How can one not know that in a healthy body, the various great elements do not encroach upon one another?

This is simply because the various great elements have ceased their mutual usurpation and returned to their original nature and source. Why is it that this very form, which is empty, is so vividly manifest before us, yet people remain deluded?

Delusion consists in clinging to the body as being existent. Alas! This is indeed a profound form of sleep. As for the fact that external forms, such as mountains and rivers, are identical with emptiness, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* speaks of this:
"Observe the nature of earth: its coarse aspect constitutes the four great elements, while its subtle aspect consists of minute particles.
Even down to the *paramāṇu* (the smallest particle), when one analyzes those ultimate atoms to their very limits of form, they are found to be composed of seven parts. Furthermore...

When one analyzes the neighboring atoms (*paramāṇu*), that which remains is the actual nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). What is called the "actual nature of emptiness" is not produced by causes and conditions;

it is the emptiness extracted through analysis, and this is precisely emptiness itself. People today perceive mountains and rivers as the composite appearance of atoms, rather than perceiving mountains and rivers as the intrinsic nature of atoms;
therefore, they see them as having substantial obstruction. How could they know that a single atom is empty?
Therefore, the collection of atoms is empty; because the collection of atoms is empty, a single atom is empty. Within the emptiness of a single atom, there is no collection of atoms;
within the emptiness of a collection of atoms, there is no single atom. Mountains and rivers are quiescent; this principle is fundamentally thus.
All you people, try to observe this quietly and investigate it in silence. How does it appear? If you can truly realize that form is itself emptiness, and that emptiness is itself form—

Form (*rūpa*) goes without saying. If one does not understand and realize such emptiness-form (*śūnyatā-rūpa*), how could one possibly give rise to the contemplative observation that emptiness and form are non-different?
Therefore, these two phrases serve to reveal the principle of their non-difference.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
This example treats the four mental aggregates as being like the aggregate of form;

it causes one to understand each of them individually as having the characteristic of emptiness, thereby giving rise to the contemplative observation that they are not different from the emptiness of the aggregates. That feeling itself is emptiness is, for example, like seeing with the eyes.
Regarding form: when one perceives a form-image, that constitutes feeling (*vedanā*). Now, when one eye sees various forms, those various forms are perceived simultaneously.
If they were not to be perceived, there would be no perception at all; thus, while this form is within the sphere of feeling, how could that form be accommodated?
Yet, when one eye sees various forms, each and every one is perceived, and there is never any obstruction to their being perceived.
One who understands this realizes that sensation (*vedanā*) is itself emptiness. As for "conception (*saṃjñā*) is itself emptiness":

to recollect immeasurable matters in a single thought-moment and to maintain a clear memory of each and every thing constitutes conception. If conception were not empty, then even a single matter would remain fixed in memory.
Regarding other matters, what could serve as a condition for them to arise? Yet, while the affairs of the donkey have not yet departed, the affairs of the horse have already arrived.
It is like a person who has gone abroad as a traveler and, after being long separated from his hometown, suddenly gives rise to a thought;

he then perceives his original homeland, his father, sons, and relatives, and all manner of worldly affairs manifesting themselves all at once. If it were not for this thinking, they would simply be empty. Can [this not be so]?
Is there such mutual integration? Sensation (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) are fundamentally empty; mental formations (saṃskāra) and consciousness (vijñāna) can be understood accordingly.

That which actively engages in sensation and perception constitutes "formations," while that which presides over these formations is "consciousness. These four are different names for the same essence. By realizing the emptiness of this single aggregate, one may awaken to the fact that all aggregates are empty.
If you wish for a clear explanation of the Dharma, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* contains the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the ten... [text fragment].
The two bases, the eighteen realms, the original Tathāgatagarbha, and the wondrous nature of True Suchness—these passages may be verified in the scriptures.

The reason those texts are not cited here is that they speak of the false to reveal the true, thereby manifesting the meaning of "separation" (li). Here, however, one must realize that the true is devoid of falsehood;

only then does the meaning of "identity" (ji) obtain. Although it can be separated, it is also capable of being identical. Yet, through separation, one attains the purity of severing delusion; whereas through identity, [one realizes the essence].
One attains the realization of true purity; without realizing the truth, one cannot sever delusion. This refers to those who study the cultivation of the mind:
they must realize that by following [the path], they immediately attain liberation from it. If one speaks only of "liberation," the person will separately form a conceptualization of liberation;

this is already delusion. How, then, can one eternally leave behind all delusions? Therefore, regarding the cultivation of the mind within the Dharma-gates, such persons are rare. Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā...
If that which is rarely heard in the world were to undergo the contemplative observation of "form being identical to emptiness," it too would have long been buried in the dust.

Yet, the state where all is identical to emptiness, where all is empty and entirely detached, where all detachment is awakening, where all awakening is clarity, where all clarity is wondrous—this which manifests within the daily activities of people, they fail to perceive when spoken of in its totality. How tragic!
Śāriputra, this is to reveal the true reality of ultimate emptiness, so that one shall not be deluded by appearances while being deluded regarding the illumination. Furthermore,
he addresses the recipient of the teaching by name once more, for sentient beings have lost the source of illumination due to their failure to understand.
Having realized the purity of the true reality (*dharmatā*), they perceive the arising of various marks (*nimitta*) and give rise to deluded攀緣 (*ālambana*).
Because their cognitive vision does not cease, they lose the *prajñā* of their own nature and revolve in samsara through inversion.

Thus, they practice with delusion and wander in the birth and death of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), following the gradual stages of the Three Vehicles, and fail to enter the lineage of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna-gotra*). Now, I shall speak to them of the profound *prajñā*.
This illuminates the emptiness of all phenomena, causing them to awaken to and practice the Mahāyāna.
If one were to teach only the emptiness of phenomena without demonstrating the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of that emptiness, they would inevitably conceptualize that "all these phenomena are empty.

When asked what the mark of this emptiness of phenomena is, they would seek its mark but fail to find it, thereby giving rise to doubt and being unable to practice the profound *prajñā* that clearly illuminates all phenomena.

All are empty. Therefore, the subsequent revelation of the characteristics of emptiness is of particular importance. He specifically calls out [the disciple’s] name to address him, causing him to alert his mind and listen attentively.
Upon hearing the characteristics of the emptiness of all phenomena, he will clearly realize the emptiness of all phenomena and attain an unerring illumination.
These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
This directly reveals the true mark of ultimate emptiness. "These dharmas" refers to the empty dharmas of the aggregates that are being pointed out and illuminated.
"The characteristic of emptiness" is the characteristic of the emptiness of all dharmas. Indeed, there exists a true emptiness; it possesses its own reality.
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Sentient beings do not awaken to true emptiness precisely because they do not perceive the true mark;

thus, they become deluded regarding clarity and lose their illumination. Within the darkness of empty obscurity, they bind darkness into form and perceive the various marks of the root-body and the vessel-world.
Failing to enter pure awakening, this [text] points them out here to bring about understanding. As for "non-arising," it is because emptiness is not something produced.
There is. That which is non-extinguished: emptiness cannot be destroyed or shattered. That which is non-defiled: emptiness does not undergo defilement. That which is non-pure:
emptiness does not undergo purification. That which does not increase: emptiness has nothing further to be added. That which does not decrease: emptiness has nothing to be removed.
Therefore, transcending cause and effect, and transcending cultivation and realization, this state of equal and pervasive fulfillment is true emptiness.

The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Upon realizing this true mark, one naturally does not give rise to illumination by being identical to form (*rūpa*), nor does one give rise to illumination by departing from form;
rather, one gives rise to illumination precisely without differing from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and without differing from form. This is because taking form itself as the mark.

The characteristic of the true nature (*dharmatā*) is that it is neither born, nor defiled, nor increased. In what [sense] is it "form" (*rūpa*)? It takes the departure from form as its characteristic.

The characteristic of the true nature is that it is neither extinguished, nor pure, nor diminished. How can one depart from form? There is nothing to which one can adhere, and nothing from which one can depart.
Perfectly luminous and non-abiding—does this not occur at this very moment? Therefore, the revelation of this true nature is precisely for the purpose of accomplishment.
This refers to the *prajñā* of illumination. To explain it analytically: it is "neither arising nor ceasing," as it is free from the cause and effect of ordinary beings;

it is "neither defiled nor pure," as it is free from the cultivation and realization of the Two Vehicles; it is "neither increasing nor decreasing," as it enters into the perfect and eternal nature of awakening. The subsequent passages provide the detailed exposition, while this section serves as the foundational inference for that explanation.
Thus, this serves as the heading pointing toward the One True [Mind], while the following sections demonstrate the departure from all delusions, thereby making known that which is illuminated.
One truly knows the delusion that must be abandoned; subsequently, one can rely on the true to revolve away from the delusive. When delusion is abandoned, it is itself the true;
thus, both are not lost within the luminous illumination. Therefore:
The preceding passage has clearly pointed out that all phenomena are characterized by emptiness; to elaborate further through extensive discourse:
the true mark of original enlightenment is the ocean of great quiescent extinction, the single source of both sentient beings and Buddhas, ultimately pure and free from all delusive appearances.

Therefore, this is the transition. "Therefore" means that because these [characteristics] such as non-arising and non-ceasing are the mark of emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*).
Within emptiness, there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; and there is no form, sound, or odor.
"From the realm of taste, touch, and mental objects, up to the realm of the eye, and so forth, up to the realm of consciousness—there is no wisdom and no attainment.

This passage, ending with the phrase "no wisdom and no attainment," collectively reveals the true mark (*dharmatā*), which is the very nature of all those delusive phenomena that have been eliminated.

Regarding the phrase "within emptiness": it means "within the true mark of emptiness. These two characters [“空” *kōng* and “中” *zhōng*] are connected with the preceding characters [“是故” *shìgù*], directly extending through to...

The phrase "no ignorance and no attainment" reveals that within the true reality of emptiness, all deluded appearances are utterly transcended and all sentient beings are fundamentally enlightened from the beginning;
there is none who does not abide on the shore of nirvana by means of the light of prajñā.
Now, these—the aggregates, bases, and elements—are the dharmas of the cycle of existence for ordinary beings.

That there is no form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness means that within the true mark (*dharmatā*), there are no phenomena characterized as the five aggregates. That there are no eyes, ears, and so forth means that within the true mark, there are no phenomena characterized as the six sense faculties.
That there are no forms, sounds, and so forth means that within the true mark, there are no phenomena characterized as the six sense objects.

The six faculties and the six objects are also called the twelve bases (*āyatana*). If one encounters many who are deluded regarding material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and few who are deluded regarding mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), then these twelve bases are pointed out for instruction. This is because the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body are all internal matter (*rūpa*).
Form, sound, odor, taste, and touch are all external forms; by now distinguishing them and pointing them out, one will not become deluded regarding them.
As for the two—mind and phenomena—they constitute mental factors (*caitta*). This refers to them as "mental factors" because there is some slight delusion concerning them.

If one encounters someone who is deluded regarding mental factors, then one should point out and reveal the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), specifically identifying them as feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Because it is a mental dharma (*caitta-dharma*). "Mind" (*manas*) refers to the mind-faculty (*manendriya*). "Dharmas" (*dharma*) refer to the reflections of the five external sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

Since the mind-faculty has no separate substantial entity, its characteristics are established in dependence upon the five faculties, such as the eye and ear. Therefore, the objects corresponding to these faculties are precisely the objects belonging to the five [faculties], such as the eye;
however, while the eye and others correspond to the specific, the mind-faculty corresponds to the general. While the eye and others correspond to present objects, the mind-faculty...

To eliminate the dust of falling away, a distinct name for the Dharma is established. "There is no eye-element, up to and including no mind-consciousness-element" means that there are no phenomena characterized by the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The phrase "up to and including" encompasses the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*), the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñāna-dhātu*), the ear-element (*śrotra-dhātu*), and so forth.

The sphere of sound, the sphere of ear-consciousness; the sphere of nose, the sphere of fragrance, the sphere of nose-consciousness; the sphere of tongue, the sphere of taste, the sphere of tongue-consciousness;

the sphere of body, the sphere of tangibles, the sphere of body-consciousness; the sphere of mind, and the sphere of phenomena—these are all fully manifested within as the eighteen spheres (*dhātus*).
As for "sphere" (*dhātu*), it carries the meaning of limitation, in the sense that one cannot transcend it. Regarding the "eye-sphere," the eye takes form as its [object].
Regarding the "element" (*dhātu*): the eye cannot see sound, fragrance, and so forth; nor can the eye transcend form (*rūpa*) to see.
As for the "form element" (*rūpadhātu*), form takes the eye as its element, because sound, fragrance, and so forth cannot confront the eye, and form must necessarily be seen by the eye.

The visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) refers to the consciousness of the eye, which takes the eye and visible forms as its constituent elements (*dhātu*). This is because consciousness first arises in dependence upon the sense organ;
the eye cannot produce consciousness of sounds, odors, and so forth. The same applies to the elements of the ear and the other senses.

These are what are called the mere proliferation of conventional designations and numerical categories. They are phenomena of the delusive appearances of ignorance, which are entirely absent from the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The dharmas of the aggregates, bases, and elements constitute the causes and effects of the cycle of existence for ordinary beings; they are the causes of arising and ceasing.
Since the true nature of reality is neither born nor extinguished, how could these exist therein? Therefore, they do not exist.

There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; likewise, up to and including, there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death. There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path.
This awakening to the absence of causes and conditions is the realization of the Four Noble Truths through the methods of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas. From ignorance up to old age...
From death as the twelve gates of transmigration (*pravṛtti*), up to the exhaustion of old age and death as the twelve gates of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Now, that which attains cessation through transmigration constitutes the contemplation of phenomena by the *pratyekabuddha*. Since there is now no transmigration, how could there be cessation?
Therefore it is said: "There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance," and so forth. This is the absence of *pratyekabuddhas*.

This is the Dharma. As for the phrase "and so forth," it encompasses the entire sequence: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;

name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth;
and birth conditions aging and death. When ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; when volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;

with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases;

with the cessation of birth, old age and death cease—this is the discourse on the cessation of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. There is no [other] suffering, origin, cessation, or path.

This refers to the Śrāvaka Dharma, which consists of the voice of one who is never weary of the fruit of suffering, who severs the cause of its accumulation, who aspires to the fruit of cessation, and who cultivates the cause of the path.

Indeed, the Śrāvaka perceives that all birth and death within the three realms are entirely the fruit of suffering. This fruit of suffering arises collectively from various deluded causes and conditions;
these accumulate and perfume until they form seeds. If there were no cause of accumulation, there would be no fruit of suffering. Thus, one aspires toward cessation. And...

One cultivates the path that distances oneself from worldly toil and delusive conceptualization. This very path establishes the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) based on the law of dependent origination within the gate of transmigration as perceived by the *pratyekabuddhas*;
it further establishes the two truths of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) based on the law of dependent origination within the gate of returning to extinction.
While these distinct gates and separate truths collectively constitute the perception of defilement and purity, within the true mark of emptiness, there is neither defilement nor purity.
It is impure. Upon what could it be established? Therefore, it does not exist.
There is neither wisdom nor attainment;
this absence of both subject and object in cultivation and realization is the Dharma of the Bodhisattva. "No wisdom" means there is no one who can cultivate; "no attainment" means...
There is nothing to be realized. For where there is realization, there is increase; where there is cultivation and elimination, there is decrease.
Within the true mark of emptiness, Buddhas and sentient beings are equal, perfectly pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. What is there to cultivate? What is there to realize?
Therefore, along with all bodhisattvas, both the mind that contemplates and the resultant realm sought are entirely non-existent. How profound!

The illumination and contemplation of *prajñā* is not a gate of clear vision belonging to the burning consciousness (*jvalana-vijñāna*), nor is it the arising and ceasing of mental factors, nor the functional operation of subject and object.
Therefore, at the beginning, it was declared that form and emptiness are not different; through this, the nature-realm of the Middle Way gives rise to the function of illumination.

In the middle, it was declared that the true emptiness and real mark are equal and eternally abiding; through this, the essence of illumination is established. Finally, it was declared regarding the ultimate...

Purity. To sever all delusions in profound stillness and eliminate the objects of illumination, one may hope to enter into the awakening of intrinsic nature, where the luminous, perfect, and brilliant illumination is identical to that of the Bodhisattvas who perceive all phenomena as empty while practicing the profound *prajñā*. This concludes the text;
taken together with the preceding section on "form not being different from emptiness," it serves to reveal and demonstrate the practice of the Bodhisattvas.
Regarding Prajñā: one must not conceive of it as being shallow at first and deep later. The illumination that illuminates emptiness is the illusory wisdom that arises;
this absence of wisdom and absence of attainment is for the purpose of eliminating the contemplation of illusion.
Because there is nothing to be attained.

This is the revelation of the pure original enlightenment (*viśuddha-mūla-bodhi*), which serves as the fundamental source for both the mind of the causal stage and the awakening of the fruition stage.
Those who, through ultimate initial awakening, perfect wondrous awakening, must necessarily rely upon the other shore of Prajñā.

Upon arrival, one transcends suffering and affliction; yet there is no delusion regarding causes, nor any contravention of effects. In cultivation there is no cultivation, and in realization there is no realization.

This state of non-attainment is the pure nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). Prajñā is the pure light of original enlightenment. Without the pure nature, the pure light does not arise;
without the pure light, the pure nature is not illumined. This is the single path of the Dharma, whose characteristic is as follows:

As for essence and function, there is neither self nor other. Therefore, this teaching is revealed to let it be known that the *prajñā* practiced by Bodhisattvas is an illumination and contemplation in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), and is not a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions.
Because Bodhisattvas rely on the perfection of wisdom, their minds are without hindrance; because they are without hindrance, they have no fear;
far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, they attain ultimate Nirvana.

This traces back to the preceding sentence to reveal the fundamental principle for Bodhisattvas: that as their nature gives rise to illumination, so does that illumination establish the causal cultivation of liberation.
*Śikṣā* (始覺) means ultimate awakening; *bodhi*, a Sanskrit term, here translated as "awakening";
*sattva*, a Sanskrit term, here translated as "sentient being" (*yǒuqíng*), which is the designation for one who seeks Buddha-wisdom to deliver sentient beings. Those who rely on Prajñā...
It is based on the naturally pure luminosity. As for "pāramitā," it refers to the object of purity that is illumined by that luminosity.

Therefore, "the mind is without hindrance" means that empty illumination is perfectly wondrous; one does not establish the dualistic discrimination of subject and object, nor of knowledge and vision, nor of grasping and rejecting.
"There is no fear" means there is no fear of the various forms of birth-and-death involving fragmentation and transformation.
These are all delusive objects. "To remain far removed from inverted dreams and thoughts" means to forever sever the various delusive cognitions and views of ignorance.
"Ultimate nirvāṇa" means that quiescent extinction is manifest before one, realizing the ocean of perfect enlightenment;

it is not like the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) of the two vehicles, which is a mere cessation like extinguished ashes. *Nirvāṇa* is a Sanskrit term; in this [Chinese] language, it is translated as "quiescent extinction" (*jimiè*) and also as "perfect quiescence" (*yuánjì*).
This means that having perfectly eliminated the five stages of dwelling, one attains quiescent and eternal peace; this is the ultimate fruit to which the Buddhas return.

When the texts are unified, there is no obstruction and no fear; being free from inverted perceptions, one reaches the culmination of *nirvāṇa*. This is what is meant by "crossing over all suffering and calamity."
The Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This [passage] traces back to the preceding sentence to reveal the source of all Buddhas: that their nature is perfect illumination, and that this illumination is wondrous. Thus it is established.
Establishing the fruit of realization: the perfect and wondrous enlightenment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. In the Sanskrit language, *anu* means "no";
*tara* means "above"; *sam* means "right"; *yak* means "equal"; and *bodhi* means "enlightenment. This is the supreme designation for the fruit of Buddhahood.
Herein, the single word "because" (*gu*) and the two instances of "because" in the preceding section [are explained].
The characters [are as follows]: because the phrase "non-attainment" (wude) is one, the character "one" (yi) is used; all these are terms for tracing back to the source.

Furthermore, the phrase "non-attainment" and the character "one" are the fundamental origins from which the three subsequent "because" (gu) phrases arise. This is because: from the pure nature (qingjingxing), pure light is emitted;
relying upon this pure light, one returns to illumine the pure nature. Thus, there is no illumination that gives rise to an object, and no object that is produced.
It is possible. Therefore, by eliminating all delusive objects and forever severing ignorance, one attains quiescence before one's eyes;
this is that which is practiced by all Bodhisattvas. Relying on pure light, one constantly illumines the pure nature, such that there is no longer deluded cognitive clarity;
perfect enlightenment (vimala-bodhi) is all-pervasive, and this is that which is realized as the fruit by all Tathāgatas. Thus, those who wish to encompass the fruit of enlightenment and penetrate...
This is the cause for awakening: to abandon the failure to practice and study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Those who aspire to the Buddha-way should reflect upon this.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra.
This fundamental Prajñāpāramitā penetrates cause and encompasses effect; its dharma-nature is profound and subtle, yet it is here extolled.
This is to cause them to know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by Bodhisattvas is not a "profound" that is deep only in contrast to the shallow;
rather, it is called "profound" because it is without counterpart or dependence, and does not fall within the scope of names, words, numbers, or quantities—it is the extremely profound *dharmatā*.
Therefore, those who know this do so because it is the ultimate, initial awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of perfect wondrous enlightenment.
And thus it is known. As for this "Great Divine Mantra," immeasurable dust-like afflictions (*kleśa*) are instantaneously shattered in a single moment by relying upon Prajñā;
how could such power be possible through any meager or superficial spiritual efficacy?

As for this "Great Illuminating Mantra," the ignorance and deluded darkness of distant kalpas are entirely transformed into the function of wisdom by relying upon Prajñā; how could this be reached by any inferior or limited cognition?
This unsurpassed mantra is the pure light of Prajñā; it transcends both sound and form, being as perfectly naked as empty space and encompassing the entire Dharma-realm.
Within the mundane and supramundane worlds, there is nothing whatsoever that can surpass it.
This mantra of the peerless equals is such that every dharma is pure and every dharma is Prajñā; manifesting in accordance with conditions, it is this one thing alone, and there is nothing else.
There is nothing else that can be compared to it; how could anything be its equal? Therefore it is said: "From the heavens above to the earth below, I alone am supreme.
Thus it is said: "I do not take the myriad dharmas as my companion. Alas! I go forth alone; never again shall I encounter him.

One may then speak of Prajñāpāramitā. Regarding the words of the mantra: the subsequent scriptural text provides a clear explanation, stating that because it can eliminate all suffering and is truly not false, one speaks this Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-mantra.
This is the mantra revealed for the sake of the Prajñāpāramitā. First it says, "The truth that removes suffering," and later it says, "Therefore, the mantra is spoken.
This is because all sufferings, calamities, and the myriad phenomena of worldly toil (*kleśa*) are established through what is termed conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Now, by relying upon Prajñā, one destroys worldly toil, transcends suffering and calamity, and realizes the truth.
Prajñā is not a mantra in the sense of a mere incantation; it is the primordial sound of purification. How, then, can it destroy conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and linguistic designations?
This is precisely what is meant by the saying: "Upon hearing [the teaching], the cataracts of the faculties are removed.
Therefore, he first declares the reality that removes suffering, and subsequently declares that Prajñā is taught as a mantra. "Therefore" means because it truly removes suffering. It is the truth.
"Substantial and not empty" refers to Prajñā. It truly and effectively removes suffering and calamity, leading to ultimate Nirvana;
it is not like fashioning flowers from the sky to produce fruit from the void. Since Prajñā is a mantra, it consists merely of names and words, possessing no substantial meaning whatsoever.
Thus, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "Know that my teaching of the Dharma is like the parable of the raft. Even the Dharma...

One should abandon [even] what is appropriate, let alone that which is contrary to the Dharma. The *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda*) states: "The teachings of the sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon.
If one sees the moon, one realizes that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon itself.

If one does not understand this, then upon hearing the teaching of Prajñā, one will again cling to it as being truly real and seek the characteristics of dharmas elsewhere, thereby becoming even more deluded. Up to this point, the text is correct; from the beginning, the name was invoked.
Having finished explaining and revealing [the meaning],
he then spoke the mantra: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.

This is the direct revelation of the mantra of Prajñā. If sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age bring this to mind through focused recollection, they will not follow after the worldly proliferation of conceptual names and terms, nor will they flow along with the stream of sounds.

Thus, their hearing becomes perfectly pure, their auditory faculty attains universal penetration, and they traverse the path to Nirvana. Because there are such benefits, the mantra is now spoken. Therefore, as for the purpose of the mantra:
It is taken to be *prajñā*. To preserve the original Sanskrit term, it remains untranslated.

It is indeed *prajñā*, for it does not fall within the realm of names, words, meanings, or truths. Although there is speaking, there has never been anything spoken; it can be heard, yet there is nothing heard.
In the preceding sutra text, the *prajñā* was taught explicitly; here, it is taught cryptically.
This is the same principle found in many Mahāyāna sūtras, where both the explicit and the cryptic are simultaneously revealed. Alas!

This sutra begins by manifesting the Dharma through the Bodhisattvas who have heard, contemplated, and cultivated [the teachings], and concludes with dhāraṇī-mantras to preserve the teaching. Yet, people today spend their whole days seeking *prajñā*, yet remain deluded.
As for Prajñā, in what does one become deluded? One cannot leap out of the circles and patterns of names and words. I pray that all sentient beings will urgently seek to turn back [from delusion].
The Heart Sūtra: Opening and Deliverance, Volume (End).
